title: Strategy games: AI to control players
author: Mobely
selftext: I have not seen anyone using ai to control the computer opponents in a strategy game. Is anyone doing this? Either on their own games or retro-fitting existing games.

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
I think, the main issue is that decision trees already work well and are much cheaper, both in terms of money and in terms of computer resources. 

That being said, i do think there is a place for llm here. 

The first place is in negotiation. Computers suck at negotiating. They struggle with subjective value. Typically in games rhat have trading or negotiation there is like a fair value and pile stuff up til you hit equal too or greater than and it makes the deal. 

Llm, has the potential for making negotiation more, complex because even though it doesn’t really understand subjective value if it’s trained in data of humans making those decisions it could mimic it. 

The other place is in communicating the decision trees decision to the player. In strategy games alot of times u do x acts and an aggression meter or something fills up and you get a stock message like, “it’s war!” But llm has the potential to craft the message based on what you actually did, in a more natural than fill in the blank way. It can insult you, it can goad you.

comments.author: Writer_IT
comments.body:
Tried It. The issue i found out, was that llm decision tended to be strictly worse than standard game ai.
And as other said, wiring in a Frontier llm would not be worth it.
If you want to have "live" characters playing with you, better to give them tools to prioritize certain tasks or attitudes (defensive, aggressive, support..) and let the usual ai evaluation algoritms take care of the actual moves.

replies.author: Vindelator
replies.body:
This is my experience too. 

When you take a relatively finite set of actions or choices to make in given situation, haven't a big fat LLM pick one vs an old school AI script or something, you don't gain a lot for all the tokens being burned.

I've built a system in my game, however, that saves replays. Someday, I want to experiment with shoving a bunch of gameplay data into an LLM and see if it can come up with interesting AI scripts.

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
I made this game and I told Sekai (it was my first Ai language model tool at the time) to have the other spaceships pursue the player ship, but if the player warps then they are cut off and the entity is removed. Well, I thought it would be just that and call it a day.

 So, during testing I noticed they would pursue no matter what distance you went, and after a long time I got to testing the damage scale, and its when I noticed the enemy would try to pursue the player even when they weren't moving, so they just flew in circles around the player infinitely and would never stop to aim or shoot! I never did finish the game and published it free if you want to see, but since I couldn't figure out how to pause when docking at another ship and pirates couldn't damage you, I left in the shitty Ai pilots so you never had to worry about getting shot while landing on a planet or docking on a ship.

comments.author: Bed-After
comments.body:
Certainly not a live AI agent, that would be ENORMOUSLY expensive, and offer no real benefit. Possibly even a downgrade. But as in having an AI write the behavior scripts for enemies, yeah, that's pretty easy to implement. 

The thing is, AI agents receive data, think on it for a second, then output a result. It's pretty easy to do that turn by turn, and refine its logic with each iteration until you get something you're happy with. Sending every single input to a data center, having it process the data, and return a response, would add a crazy amount of latency, and allow AI hallucinations and mistakes to creep into what could have been a simple and concise behavior script.

comments.author: Matilozano96
comments.body:
There have been machine learning experiments with games.

I remember OpenAI published an experiment around DOTA some years back:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI\_Five

There’s probably similar RTS experiments here and there.

For what I gather from googling papers, RTSs just have too many variables compared to a MOBA; so the training process would be a lot more costly.

Where the research is right now, it’s probably not feasible to run ML systems for an RTS’ AI. It would tank the system’s performance too much for it to be worth it.
